procedure: Take the class to a playground where a see-saw is available.
Let a lighter child sit on the left side and a heavier child on the right side of the see-saw, at equal distances from the pivot.
Observe whether the heavier child moves down.
Move the heavier child nearer to the pivot and the lighter child away from the pivot.
Observe the direction in which the see-saw tilts and which child moves down.
aim: To observe how the turning effect of a force depends on the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot.

viva.question: What is the turning effect of a force called?
What is the moment arm of a force?
viva.answer: The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.

viva.question: What is the line of action of a force?
viva.answer: The line along which the force acts.

viva.question: How does increasing the moment arm affect the turning effect?
Why does the heavier child move down when both children are equally far from the pivot?
viva.answer: The heavier child exerts a greater downward force, producing a greater turning effect.

viva.question: Why are door handles fitted far from the hinges?
viva.answer: A larger moment arm produces a greater turning effect with less force.

diagram: Draw a see-saw with a lighter child on the left and a heavier child on the right, a central pivot, downward arrows showing the forces, and the perpendicular distances from the pivot labelled “Moment arm” on both sides; label the pivot “Pivot”.
title: Turning effect of force on a see-saw
precautions: Use a stable see-saw and keep its pivot clear of obstructions.
Children should sit securely and hold the see-saw handles, if provided.
Move the children gradually and keep them seated while the see-saw is in motion.
Keep other students at a safe distance from the moving see-saw.
result: With the children at equal distances from the pivot, the heavier child moves down. When the heavier child moves nearer the pivot and the lighter child farther away, the see-saw tilts in the opposite direction, showing that the turning effect depends on both the force and its moment arm.
